ECE 6390

From look angle to satellite scan angle

From the figure to the concept

Fig. 1 shows the Earth–GEO segment to a station at 33.75° N drawn to scale, with the station’s 50.8° elevation and the satellite antenna’s 5.49° scan away from nadir.

A ground station and a satellite share one physical segment but describe it from opposite ends. In a common Earth-fixed frame, the station’s unit vector toward the satellite is q̂_g = (r_s − r_g)/R, where R is the slant range. The satellite’s unit vector toward the station is q̂_s = −q̂_g. Reverse the ray first, then express it in the local axes each end uses.

The station projects q̂_g onto its local east, north and up axes: elevation El = asin(q̂_g·û) and azimuth Az = atan2(q̂_g·ê, q̂_g·n̂). The satellite projects q̂_s onto its antenna axes: the scan angle from the antenna normal is θ_scan = acos(q̂_s·ẑ_s), and the direction cosines u_x = q̂_s·x̂_s and u_y = q̂_s·ŷ_s locate the station in the array pattern.

The two angles answer different questions. Elevation tells the ground antenna where to point and how much atmosphere the path crosses. Scan angle tells which part of the satellite pattern serves that station, and therefore which gain belongs in the link budget. For a nadir-facing antenna, the triangle formed by Earth’s centre, the station and the satellite gives sin θ_scan = (r_e/r_s) cos El, so the whole visible Earth lies within about 8.7° of nadir from GEO.

Aiming the antenna normal at a chosen point changes ẑ_s and therefore every station’s scan angle, while the ground elevations stay the same. A phased array chooses that pointing electronically; a fixed reflector chooses it mechanically.

Example

For a station at 33.75° N on the satellite’s meridian, q̂_g in east–north–up components is about (0, −0.633, 0.774), so El = 50.76° and Az = 180°. The slant range is 37,031 km. A nadir-facing antenna sees the reversed ray at u_y = −0.0957 and θ_scan = 5.49°; aiming the normal at the station makes the scan zero.

Practice

1. A station sees a GEO satellite at 0° elevation, on its horizon. What scan angle does a nadir-facing satellite antenna see?

Use sin θ_scan = (r_e/r_s) cos El with r_e = 6378 km and r_s = 42,164 km.

sin θ_scan = 6378/42,164 ≈ 0.151, so θ_scan ≈ 8.70°. This is the edge of the Earth disk seen from GEO.

2. Why is the satellite scan angle not 90° minus the ground elevation?

Compare the two reference directions: the station’s local up and the satellite’s nadir.

Elevation is measured from the station’s horizon, while scan is measured from the satellite’s antenna normal. Those references are not parallel—they meet at Earth’s centre—so the angles are related through the Earth-centred triangle rather than a simple complement.
